notes.title: Bloomberg Businessweek's Big Take quotes Della Vedova on where insider trading concentrates
notes.body: Denitsa Tsekova and Leonardo Nicoletti analyze 34,000 Polymarket trades flagged as potential insider activity: roughly $200 million in flagged volume from January through June 2026, driven by bets on military action in Iran and Venezuela. Winnings were heavily concentrated, with the top 1% of profitable wallets capturing more than half the money; 57% of those wallets were created less than 24 hours before trading. The piece quotes our assessment of where private-information trading concentrates: elections, committee decisions, award shows, ballot measures, and government votes, the markets where a small group knows the outcome first. Their category-level findings match that ordering; financial and economic markets showed the least flagged activity.

notes.title: The Atlantic quotes Della Vedova on 'outsider trading' after the Paris hair-dryer incident
notes.body: Kaitlyn Tiffany's July 20 piece examines a new class of prediction-market conduct: winning a bet by changing the world instead of forecasting it. In April a Météo-France sensor near Charles de Gaulle jumped 4 degrees Celsius in twelve minutes; a wallet positioned above the 21-degree strike against an 18-degree consensus collected roughly $20,000, and Météo-France filed a criminal complaint. Polymarket changed its data source but let the winnings stand; France ordered internet providers to block the site on July 16. The article quotes our recommendations: screen for excess accuracy (a wallet betting one song hits No. 1 while betting no on every rival shows confidence the market's prices cannot explain, whether it comes from an inside line or rigged streams), limit bet sizes where results are cheap to rig, and never resolve a market from a single number at a single source. The trader who rigs the sensor never out-forecasts anyone; the same trade-record footprint our insider-timing and resolution-surprise indices flag gives them away.

notes.title: Flagged wallets: mostly retail by count, almost entirely bots by dollars.
notes.body: Of 6,291 wallets flagged at p<0.01 by the wallet-level detection test, 62% are active retail, 21% are sophisticated, only 16% are algorithmic. But profitability tells the opposite story: 4,306 (68.4%) of the flagged set were profitable, generating $152.5M in aggregate. The 1,026 flagged bots captured $137.6M of that — 90% of all flagged-wallet gains flow to the algorithmic 16%, with mean PnL of $134K per bot vs $2.2K per retail wallet. The wallet-level screen finds statistical patterns consistent with informed trading across every wallet class; the dollars accrue almost entirely to the algos who can act on it at scale.

notes.title: Paper 2 revised: per-event detection test, CFTC case validation.
notes.body: Revised version of Paper 2 posted to SSRN under a new title: "Detecting Informed Trading in Prediction Markets: One Event at a Time." The revision replaces the wallet-level screen with a per-event joint-accuracy test, multiplicity-corrected across a trader's events. Calibrated on a real-data placebo where episodic private information is implausible — the corrected test yields zero discoveries at every threshold. Applied to the trader charged in CFTC v. Spagnuolo (2026), the test shows statistical patterns consistent with informed trading where every trader-aggregated statistic does not.

notes.title: Paper 2 posted to SSRN
notes.body: "Detecting Informed Trading in Prediction Markets" posted to SSRN (abstract_id 6567238). Uses the theta-epsilon framework from Paper 1 as a detection signal. 6,292 of 483K wallets show statistical patterns consistent with informed trading at p<0.01. (Superseded by the June 2026 revision, 'One Event at a Time': the wallet-level statistic is reclassified as a sustained-skill measure; see the June 18 note.)
